sentences.text: The primary fossil specimen is incomplete, missing the skull but retaining vertebrae, a humerus, and a fragment of the pubic bone.
A second, smaller partial skeleton was later assigned to the same genus.
Scientists identified nine unique derived traits, known as autapomorphies, that are specific to this animal.
Vertical ridges on the front tail vertebrae fuse at their lower ends to create a V-shaped structure.
The upper edge of the humerus is nearly three times wider than the diameter of the shaft.
The upper width of the first metatarsal bone exceeds its length.
The claws on the toes are reduced, rough, and cut short in appearance.
The foot displays a unique build that is rarely preserved in sauropod fossils.
The animal possesses truncated unguals, a characteristic otherwise unknown in the Sauropoda.
Researchers noted nine distinct derived features unique to this species.
The foot shows a unique constitution, as this part of the skeleton is seldom preserved in sauropods.
Notocolossus possessed a compact and homogeneous metatarsus, believed to be adapted to support its extraordinary weight.
This dinosaur held the record for the largest Cretaceous sauropod humerus until 2026, when a larger one was found in Nagatitan.
Scientists estimated the total femur length to be exactly 2.166 meters.
Based on body proportions, the animal likely weighed between 44.9 and 75.9 tonnes, with 60.4 tonnes being the most probable estimate.
It is estimated to have weighed between 44.9 and 60.4 tonnes and measured between 25 and 32 meters in length.
The humerus measures 1.76 meters, making it longer than the known humerus of any other titanosaurian.
The foot claws are reduced, blunt, and truncated, a feature unknown among other sauropods.
The fossil remains were discovered in Mendoza province by Argentine paleontologist Dr. Bernardo Javier González Riga.
The species Notocolossus gonzalezparejasi was formally named and described in 2016 by a team led by Dr. González Riga.
Fossils were discovered by Dr. Bernardo Javier González Riga in Mendoza Province and published in 2016.
The genus name combines Greek words for "south" and "giant statue," referencing the animal's Southern Hemisphere origin and massive size.
The holotype specimen UNCUYO-LD 301 was found in strata of the Plottier Formation dating from the Coniacian to Santonian ages.
A second specimen, UNCUYO-LD 302, represents a smaller individual with five anterior caudal vertebrae and a complete, articulated foot, an exceptional find for any sauropod.
Evidence suggests Notocolossus was among the largest titanosaurs and one of the heaviest land animals ever discovered.
The ecosystem of the Plottier Formation included mammals, a large coelurosaur, and several titanosaur species.
Tetrapods from the Plottier Formation are poorly known and include mammals, a large ceratosaurian, and several titanosaurians.
A 2016 cladistic analysis placed Notocolossus within Titanosauria, in the group Lithostrotia, as a basal taxon sister to Dreadnoughtus.
A 2017 study placed Notocolossus outside of Lithostrotia as the sister taxon of Lognkosauria.
A 2018 study placed Notocolossus within Lognkosauria in a polytomy with Patagotitan and Puertasaurus.
In 2018, González Riga and colleagues determined that Notocolossus belonged to Lognkosauria, in a polytomy with Patagotitan and Puertasaurus.
Notocolossus lived during the late Cretaceous in Mendoza Province, Argentina.
Notocolossus lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, 86 million years ago, in what is now Argentina.
Notocolossus lived from the Coniacian to the Santonian, approximately 89.8 to 83.6 million years ago.
